parsed.explanation: Combined regime: a strongly protective state/province nested inside a hostile national government. Locally, gender identity is constitutionally protected, public accommodations are enforceable, gender-neutral bathrooms are mandated, the arrest-weaponised loitering statute and panic defence are repealed, and hate-crime coverage plus shield laws operate — documented, working protections with high public support. Nationally, entry is the sharpest exposure: X markers barred, passports/visits fixed to birth sex, officers told to refuse on 'reasonable doubt' about sex with possible lifetime fraud ineligibility, travellers report blocked passports and foreign advisories; federal buildings exclude trans users; federal and immigration custody apply conversion-therapy-style policies and documented abuse. Litigation is pending, but the passport regime is already in force. Everyday street life is safe; discovery at the border or in federal custody is not.

entry_documents.exposure: National regime (EO Jan 2025; passport restrictions allowed to take effect Nov 2025): X markers and non-birth-sex markers barred on passports/visas; Feb 2025 cable tells officers to refuse where documents cast 'reasonable doubt' on sex and to weigh fraud-based lifetime ineligibility. Travellers report blocked/confiscated passports and being stranded; eight-plus governments issued advisories.
entry_documents.protection: No state-level document friction for visitors; legal-aid FAQ advises on document rules. State cannot override federal border authority.
entry_documents.interaction: State acceptance of identity is irrelevant at the federal counter; document discrepancy can escalate into refusal, investigation and custody.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal corrections bureau adopted (2026) conversion-therapy-style policies for transgender inmates: hair cut, hormones removed, psychiatric substitution; prisoner counts no longer published. Transgender men in immigration custody reported forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse by guards. A visitor detained over document issues enters this system.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: State repealed the statute police used to arrest trans people (2021) and repealed the gay/trans panic defence (2019); state custody practice for visitors not separately documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Federal custody exposure is unreachable by state shield statutes; state protections end where federal detention begins.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Federal order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; nationally 21 units restrict facility use and 4 criminalise it in some circumstances (none is this state). A trans arrest for restroom use occurred in another unit (March 2025).
federal_state_facilities.protection: State sits in the 15-member 'Most Protective' tier; no facility ban; gender-neutral bathrooms mandated since 2021; public accommodations covered by the 2019 discrimination act and 2024 constitutional amendment, enforced by the Division of Human Rights.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal buildings inside the state follow the federal exclusion even while state and private premises are protected.

care_services.exposure: Federal orders frame youth care as 'mutilation', restrict funding, and DOJ subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for under-19 patient records; proposed rules would bar public-insurance reimbursement. How state shields interact with this federal pressure is not addressed in the dossier.
care_services.protection: State shield law (2023), city executive order (June 2023) and municipal ordinances protect patients and providers from out-of-jurisdiction charges — expressly relevant to visitors travelling from ban jurisdictions — and bar law-enforcement cooperation.
care_services.interaction: State shield protects the visit itself but offers nothing after the traveller returns or if federal authorities act.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Federal framing is hostile: DOJ memo invoking 'radical gender ideology' among extremist viewpoints (though not as a reward criterion), May 2026 counterterrorism strategy naming groups 'radically pro-transgender', care described as mutilation, orders to investigate schools; advocates compare the trajectory to genocide's early stages.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: State level: 2024 constitutional amendment banning gender-identity discrimination, hate-crime statute covering gender identity since 2019, DHR enforcement, 82% public support for non-discrimination (2022, LGBTQ-general).
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Federal threat-framing raises the stakes of any encounter with federal, not state, agents.

minors_guardians.exposure: Federal orders target trans minors: care called mutilation, funding freeze, directive to investigate and prosecute educators facilitating social transition, DOJ subpoenas of under-19 medical records; a visiting minor's passport faces the same marker regime.
minors_guardians.protection: State conversion-therapy ban (2019), shield law protecting families seeking care here from out-of-state custody-removal orders, anti-bullying law covering gender identity, self-affirmation marker changes with parental consent.
minors_guardians.interaction: Care sought in this state is protected locally but remains exposed to federal funding, subpoena and insurance rules.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Not documented. The dossier explicitly records no trans-specific violence incident and no rate comparable to a general homicide baseline in this state.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Documented: Hate Crimes Act covering gender identity/expression since 2019 with 2022 reforms, panic-defence repeal (2019), repeal of the statute used to harass trans people (2021), public accommodations coverage.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: State recourse operates in parallel with federal hostility, which does not reach street crime response.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Federal remedies are incomplete: several orders enjoined but the passport restriction is in force after the November 2025 Supreme Court order; the ACLU-style suit remains unresolved, so exposure varies by moment of travel. Shield/ federal-healthcare interaction unresolved; state remedy availability to non-resident visitors not spelled out.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Pending litigation, legal-aid FAQ, Division of Human Rights complaint process, shield statutes, 'Most Protective' ranking and follow-up enforcement machinery documented.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: State remedies work for services and violence; border and federal-custody harms have only litigation as recourse.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.35-A has a nationwide birth-sex bathroom rule upheld by courts with no relief and document checks on appearance. Here the facility exclusion is federal-scope only, while the state mandates gender-neutral bathrooms, protects public accommodations and enforces them — lower local exposure. But our entry/document regime is heavier: marker refusal plus fraud-based lifetime ineligibility, which 0.35-A lacks. Net slightly above 0.35-A.

0.55-B's parent has no presentation offence or facility restriction; local hostility is only partially remedied. Our local climate is far better documented as protective, but our parent imposes documented universal exposures (federal facility exclusion, marker-fixed documents, visa refusals) and custody abuse with no effective remedy. Better locally, worse at the border and in custody — comparable overall, with a different risk shape.

0.75-C features a dead-letter statute, accepted documents, community acceptance and enforced compensation, with only an open custody question. Ours has none of that passivity: an operative federal document regime, federal facility exclusion and documented custody harm. Materially below 0.75-C despite stronger written state protections, because tier-1 exposures are live rather than latent.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets two regimes in sequence. At entry, the federal layer dominates: marker-fixed documents, officer discretion to refuse on 'reasonable doubt' about sex, fraud-based lifetime ineligibility, blocked passports and foreign travel advisories — documented, in force, and unremedied despite pending litigation. Inside the state, the picture inverts: constitutional non-discrimination, enforceable public accommodations, mandated gender-neutral facilities, hate-crime coverage, shield laws protecting visiting families seeking care, repeal of the arrest-weaponised statutes, and high public support. The exposure concentrates at the boundary and in federal enclaves — federal buildings, federal and immigration custody with conversion-therapy-style policies and documented abuse — and in the pending but not yet effective court challenges. Everyday street and service encounters are comparatively safe; discovery by a federal officer is where severity rises sharply. For a traveller with a minor, state shield protections for care operate, but federal framing of trans youth and the same document regime apply to the child's papers.
